7What drives the battery's profit

Three things move a battery's profit: what the battery can do (), what the prices offer (spread, length of the price events, number of alternations), and what the model assumes after (section 8). A useful decomposition to reason about the first two:

Poll — predict first

In the toy example, if the energy capacity doubles ( kWh) with the same , the profit changes from 750 DKK to…

Answer. 900 DKK, not 1 500. Only 5 more kWh can be used — two cheap hours at 10 kW cap what can be bought at 20 kWh — and they earn the next spread, DKK/kWh.

Sizing: energy against power

Battery (toy) (kWh) (kW) (h) Profit (DKK) per kWh per kW Cycles Captured spread
base 15 10 1.5 750 50 75 1.0 50
double 30 10 3 900 30 90 0.67 45
double both 30 20 1.5 1 500 50 75 1.0 50
double 15 20 0.75 900 60 45 1.0 60
  • Same duration , same profit per kWh and per kW (rows 1 and 3): scaling both is scaling the battery.
  • Longer , lower profit per kWh: energy waits for spreads that are not there. Doubling alone cut both the number of cycles and the captured spread.
  • Shorter , higher profit per kWh but lower per kW: power waits for energy.
The sizing rule

Match the duration to the length of the price event the battery lives on — as long as the peak, and no longer. In the toy, two cheap and two expensive hours at 10 kW mean that nothing beyond 20 kWh can be used: the profit caps at 900 DKK. Losses only set a minimum spread; below it the battery does nothing, whatever its size. Short peaks reward power, long peaks reward energy.

The multipliers are the sizing signals

One more kWh of capacity is worth in every hour the battery is full, and one more kW is worth the power multiplier in every saturated hour:

The second expression assumes a single power limit .

Toy (15 kWh, 10 kW) 24-h class day (25 kWh, 10 kW)
One more kWh of capacity, 30 DKK per kWh·day, until where the power limit takes over (then 0) 82 DKK per kWh·day
One more kW of power, 10 + 20 = 30 DKK per kW·day 63 DKK per kW·day

Four-hour toy. Profit against energy capacity (left) and power limit (right); the red dotted line is the base case (15 kWh, 10 kW). The profit is piecewise linear, and the sum of the relevant multipliers (blue) is its slope — valid until the next kink.

Investment reading. Invest in kWh while (per day) beats the daily annualised cost of a kWh, and in kW while beats that of a kW — the week 4 zero-profit logic for a power plant, with one multiplier per resource.

8Choosing an end-of-horizon formulation

Section 4 showed that any end condition is an assumption about the prices after . Four families of formulations make that assumption in different ways; they differ in what they guarantee at , what information they need, and which value they put on the energy left at the end.

Modelling choice Guarantee at Information used Value of stored energy at Main risk
Free end () none none 0 (nothing after is worth anything) dumps at the end
Minimum level () yes a daily pattern Lagrange multiplier — revealed myopic; infeasibility
Rolling horizon (optimise over , apply ) no a forecast of hours Lagrange multiplier — revealed, depends on the forecast forecast error
Terminal value () no one price — chosen calibration

The formulations, written out

All five share the objective , the dynamics , the power bounds – and the energy bounds – for ; they differ only in what they say about — and every one of them, through stationarity in , puts a price on the last kWh. The common block is abbreviated as –, below.

(a) Free end

Stationarity in : . Nothing after is worth anything to the model, so whenever the last hours allow it the battery sells down to and is the multiplier of the bound — the price it would have paid to have one more kWh to sell (60 DKK/kWh in the toy). If energy is left over because it cannot be sold profitably, and : the leftover is literally worthless in the model. This is the intermediate formulation of section 3 and the base case of the toy.

(b) Minimum end level

Stationarity in is unchanged, , but is now the multiplier of . The model sells down to exactly and is what the last required kWh would have earned during the day — revealed by the solver, from today's prices only (60 then 80 DKK/kWh on the toy starting full). Requires and reachability from within hours at , otherwise the LP is infeasible. The parameter is a quantity chosen from a daily pattern; the price on it is not chosen.

(c) Cyclic end

The minimum end level with : the day must end at least where it started, so the schedule can be repeated every day without drifting. Same stationarity, same reading of . Two variants are common. With an equality the multiplier is free, which would let the model be paid for ending above ; the inequality form is the safe one. And when the starting level is itself a decision — a variable with , — stationarity in gives : the value of a kWh at the start of the day equals its value at the end, which is what a steady daily cycle should give.

(d) Terminal value

(DKK/kWh, a given parameter; written on the slides) is the value the modeller assigns to every kWh left at . The term of the Lagrangian gains , so stationarity becomes : whenever , , chosen rather than revealed. The battery keeps energy it could only sell below and sells energy it can sell above ; the amount kept steps at the prices is compared with — on the toy starting full, nothing for below 60, 5 kWh for between 60 and 80, all 15 kWh above 80 (section 8, Fix 2). A decreasing value curve is the same LP with split into segments:

Because the decrease, the solver fills the segments in order without any binary variable, and equals the of the last segment in use — a value that falls with the amount kept, which is what tomorrow's marginal value actually does. Hydro producers call this curve the water value.

(e) Rolling horizon

The end condition (free or minimum level) sits at , where it matters less, and the hours are only used to price the energy carried across : by , whenever is interior, so is revealed by the forecast — it is the value a kWh would have in the forecast hours. Those hours are then decided again at the next roll with better information. The cost is a forecast of hours (forecast error replaces the horizon error) and a model times larger at every roll; the rule of section 8 is to look ahead at least one full cycle of the battery.

Formulation What changes for Stationarity in is …
(a) free end nothing: 0 if energy is left; if it ends empty
(b) minimum level , revealed from today's prices
(c) cyclic , revealed; equals when is free
(d) terminal value in the objective, , chosen (a curve with segments)
(e) rolling horizon the horizon runs to with forecast prices; the rule sits at , revealed from the forecast

All five are linear programs: strong duality and the KKT reading of sections 5–6 apply unchanged. The two-day benchmark used to judge them is formulation (a) over hours with both days' prices.

The benchmark and three metrics

If tomorrow's prices were known, the ground truth would be a single LP over both days. Each formulation is judged against it with three metrics:

  • Two-day regret = benchmark − (day 1 + day 2 continued from ): what the end condition costs once tomorrow arrives.
  • Terminal state-of-charge deviation: against the benchmark's state of charge at the end of day 1.
  • Implicit terminal price: against the benchmark's at the end of day 1 — the true value of the last kWh.

In the toy (starts full): if tomorrow repeats today, the benchmark ends day 1 empty with and earns 1 850 DKK, so any has a regret (150, 450, 750 DKK for 5, 10, 15 kWh). If tomorrow is (80, 60, 30, 20), the benchmark keeps 5–10 kWh with and earns 1 200 DKK; the free end then has a regret of 100 DKK.

Fix 1 — look ahead: the rolling horizon

Instead of guessing what the energy left at is worth, let the model see further: at each roll, optimise over hours — today's known prices followed by a forecast of the next days — apply only the first hours, and start the next roll from the energy left at (formulation (e) above). The end condition moves to , where it matters less; the hours after are only there to price the energy carried across , and they are decided again at the next roll with better information. By , whenever is interior: the forecast reveals the price of the last kWh.

Toy, starts empty, 1 2 3 4 Full-horizon optimum
Free end at 750 2 350 2 350 2 350 2 350
Cyclic end at () 750 2 000 2 000 2 000 2 350

Values in DKK over four days: day 1 = (20, 30, 60, 80) followed by three ‘expensive-first’ days (80, 60, 30, 20), kWh, kW, no losses. The full-horizon optimum is one 16-hour LP with a free end.

With the battery earns today's 750 DKK and then nothing: each following day, seen alone, has falling prices, so a one-day model never buys in its cheap evening for the next morning. With it sells only 5 kWh at 80 today and keeps 10 kWh for tomorrow's first hour, also at 80, and then, every evening, buys 15 kWh at 30 and 20 to sell them the next morning at 80 and 60: 2 350 DKK, the full-horizon optimum. Looking further ahead adds nothing here, because one full cycle of this battery fits in two days. The cyclic end at loses 350 DKK: the last roll must end where it started, full, so on the final evening the battery buys 15 kWh that it never sells — the same myopic price on the end level as in section 4, now at .

The same test on the week with a cheap weekend ([Interactive Dashboard] A battery against the prices, tab C2, 10 kW): batteries of 2 and 4 hours lose nothing with ; the 8-hour battery needs (1.9 % regret at ); the 24-hour battery has a regret of 5.0 %, 1.1 % and 0.12 % for and needs to match the full horizon. Look ahead at least one full cycle of the battery — roughly its duration plus the next price event; the longer the duration, the longer the look-ahead that still pays. A seasonal hydro reservoir looks months ahead. The costs are a forecast of hours (forecast error replaces the horizon error) and a model times larger at every roll.

Fix 2 — price the end: the terminal value

The other fix names the price instead of hiding it: add to the objective (formulation (d) above), with in DKK/kWh the value assigned to every kWh left at . The Lagrangian gains , and stationarity in becomes

A minimum end level is the same thing with the price chosen by the solver (); the terminal value is the same thing with the price chosen by the modeller. The battery keeps the energy it could only sell below and sells what it can sell above :

Day 1 does (after buying 15 kWh in hours 1–2) sells 5 kWh at 60 and 10 kWh at 80 sells 10 kWh at 80, keeps 5 kWh keeps all 15 kWh
(kWh) 0 5 15
60 () 80 ()

Two days, tomorrow = (20, 30, 60, 80) 1 500 1 350 750

Values in DKK. Day 2 is re-optimised from with a free end; the benchmarks are 1 500 and 850 DKK (section 9, where this experiment is run step by step). At and exactly the battery is indifferent and a solver may return either neighbouring schedule.

  • The right is tomorrow's value of a kWh — the that the two-day benchmark reports at the end of day 1: 60 if tomorrow repeats today, 80 if it is expensive first. Set to it and the one-day schedule matches the benchmark's first day. Would it match the day after? Only if recalibrated: is a forecast in the form of a price.
  • One price is crude when tomorrow's marginal value falls with the amount kept. Against (80, 60, 30, 20) the benchmark keeps 5 to 10 kWh: up to 10 kWh are worth 80 tomorrow (hour 5, at the power limit), anything beyond only 60 (hour 6), less than the 80 they fetch today. No single reproduces that: at the model keeps all 15 kWh and loses 100 DKK. A decreasing value curve over segments of (formulation (d), second form) fixes this — the ‘water value’ curve of hydro scheduling.
  • The risk is calibration. when tomorrow repeats today keeps everything and has a regret of 750 DKK; when tomorrow is expensive first dumps and has a regret of 100 DKK. The terminal value is fast (one LP over hours, no forecast to run) and only as good as its price.
Rule of thumb

Rolling horizon when forecasts and computation allow; terminal value when speed matters and the price can be calibrated (from a longer run, or from history); a minimum end level when feasibility after is non-negotiable — a reserve for the next morning, a contracted service. Whatever the choice, read and compare it with the benchmark's: that is the price the model has put on the future.

9Closing the horizon: the sensitivity analysis, step by step

This is block C2 of the lecture, which the session did not reach; it is covered here in full and is the optional (no-coding) homework on tab C2 of the dashboard. Section 8 listed the ways of closing the horizon and the three metrics to judge them. This section does the experiment on the toy, in the order of the slides: first what a minimum end level does to one day, then what it does once tomorrow arrives, then the two fixes — a look-ahead and a terminal value — with a sensitivity analysis of each. The battery starts empty throughout (, the base case of section 2, 750 DKK); section 4 ran the first step for a battery starting full.

The theory: the end of day 1 is a trade between today and tomorrow

Fix a closing rule — free end, , cyclic, a terminal value , or a look-ahead of days. The two-day experiment is: solve day 1 under , record the energy left and the day-1 profit ; then solve day 2 with tomorrow's prices, starting from , with a free end, and record . The benchmark is one LP over both days (formulation (a) of section 8 over hours): what the battery would earn if it saw tomorrow's prices today. Since the benchmark can reproduce any two-day schedule, it is never beaten, and the three metrics of section 8 are

To see what the benchmark does at , split it at the day boundary. Let be the best day-1 profit when exactly kWh must be left at , and the best day-2 profit when kWh are received at the start of day 2. Any two-day schedule passes through some at , so

Both functions are concave and piecewise linear, because each is the optimal value of an LP as a function of a right-hand side. Their slopes are multipliers we already know: is the marginal cost of leaving one more kWh today, the multiplier of from section 4, i.e. of the one-day model; and is the marginal value of one more kWh received tomorrow, the value of the day-2 problem (one more kWh in the battery at the start of day 2). The benchmark keeps energy at exactly as long as its value tomorrow is at least its cost today, and the common value where the two curves meet is , the true price of the last kWh. Every closing rule replaces the unknown by a guess: the free end by (tomorrow is worthless), a minimum end level by a quantity (a vertical line at ), a terminal value by the straight line (a flat marginal value ), a look-ahead by the forecast's own . The regret is the loss from optimising instead of : zero whenever the guess lands on a maximiser of the true sum, positive otherwise, and never negative.

Toy, starts empty. Left: falls at 60 DKK/kWh for the first 5 kWh kept (the sale in hour 3 given up) and at 80 beyond (hour 4); rises at 30 then 20 if tomorrow repeats today (each kWh received replaces a purchase), at 80 then 60 if tomorrow starts dear (each kWh received is sold in hour 5, then hour 6). Right: the slopes. If tomorrow repeats today, tomorrow's value (30) is below today's cost (60) from the first kWh: keep nothing, . If tomorrow starts at 80, the first 5 kWh are worth 80 tomorrow and cost 60 today (keep), the next 5 are worth 80 and cost 80 (indifferent), the last 5 are worth 60 and cost 80 (sell): to 10 kWh, .

Day 1 alone, for kWh. The battery buys 15 kWh in hours 1–2 (350 DKK) whatever the rule, then sells as much as the rule allows, in the best hours first: hour 4 at 80 (up to 10 kWh, the power limit), then hour 3 at 60.

Reading: the first 5 kWh kept cost 60 each — the hour-3 sale given up — and the next 10 cost 80 each, the hour-4 sale. That is of the figure above, and the multiplier of the end-level constraint is its slope, revealed from today's prices only. Note the free-end column: binds there too, so — the first kWh anyone would ask the battery to keep costs 60, whatever the rule. Also note that the reported at is 60, the slope to the left of the kink; the slope to the right is 80, and a solver may report either (section 7, kinks).

Step 2 — what it does once tomorrow arrives

Poll — predict first

Tomorrow's prices are (80, 60, 30, 20). Which today gives the best two-day profit: 0, 5–10 kWh, or 15 kWh?

Answer. 5 to 10 kWh (850 DKK, the benchmark). Keeping nothing earns 750 + 0: day 2 starts dear and ends cheap, so an empty battery has nothing to sell and nothing worth buying. Keeping everything also earns 750: the last 5 kWh only fetch 60 tomorrow after costing 80 today. The common mistake is C — “the prices are 80 tomorrow, keep it all” — which forgets that hour 5 can only take 10 kWh and that the 15th kWh cost 80 today.

Now day 2 is scheduled from the energy left, with a free end, for two tomorrows. If tomorrow repeats today, each kWh received replaces a purchase at 30 (the first 5) or 20 (the rest). If tomorrow is (80, 60, 30, 20), each kWh received is sold at 80 in hour 5 (up to 10 kWh) or 60 in hour 6, and nothing else happens: the battery ends the second day empty.

Tomorrow expensive first. The benchmark (blue) fills the battery on day 1, sells 5 kWh at 80 in hour 4 and carries 10 kWh across to sell at 80 in hour 5; its value of stored energy at is 80. Reading: day 1 always loses from keeping energy (60, then 80 per kWh), and whether day 2 pays it back depends on tomorrow's first prices — information the one-day model does not have. The same has a regret of 450 on one tomorrow and 0 on the other. The “right” is a forecast in disguise: a quantity that only makes sense once the price it implies ( or 80) is compared with tomorrow's marginal value (30 or 80). Section 4 reached the same conclusion for a battery starting full; the numbers there differ by the 350 DKK of the day-1 purchases and the benchmarks are 1 850 and 1 200, but the regrets are identical.

The dashboard reports, for each closing rule and each tomorrow, the regret, the terminal state-of-charge deviation (positive: ended too full; negative: too empty) and the implicit terminal price against . On the toy:

Three things to read off. First, the free end and the cyclic rule are the same here because — with a battery starting half full the cyclic rule keeps half, and on the 24-hour class day that costs 80 DKK of regret against a benchmark that ends the day empty ([Interactive Dashboard] A battery against the prices, preset C2d). Second, a rule can have zero regret with the “wrong” implicit price: reports against a benchmark value of 80, yet its regret is 0, because the benchmark is indifferent between 5 and 10 kWh — at a kink the price is an interval, and 5 kWh sits at its edge. Third, the sign of is the operational reading: too empty means the rule under-valued the energy left (raise or ), too full means it over-valued it.

Left: the two-day profit against the minimum end level is of the theory — concave, with its maximum at the benchmark's end state; every other level is regret. Right: against the terminal value the profit is a step function: is compared with the prices at which the energy could be sold today (60 for the first 5 kWh, 80 for the rest), so only three cases exist.

Step 4 — Fix 1, the look-ahead: when does stop mattering?

The rolling horizon (formulation (e) of section 8) optimises days with today's prices followed by a forecast, applies the first day, and rolls. With and a correct forecast, day 1 is simply the first half of the benchmark: on the toy it ends with 10 kWh when tomorrow is expensive first and empty when tomorrow repeats today, and the forecast has revealed or 60 — the regret is zero by construction. The sensitivity question is how far ahead one must look, and the answer depends on the battery, not on the calendar:

With it keeps 10 kWh for hour 5 and, every evening, fills up at 30 and 20 for the next morning: 2 350 DKK, the full-horizon optimum. and 4 add nothing — one full cycle of this battery fits in two days.
  • Week. Batteries of 2 and 4 hours lose nothing at : they cycle within the day. The 8-hour battery needs (1.9 % regret at ), the 24-hour battery needs to see the weekend coming: 5.0 %, 1.1 %, 0.12 % at and zero from . Rule: look ahead at least one full cycle of the battery — roughly its duration plus the next price event. A seasonal hydro reservoir looks months ahead.
  • Costs. A price forecast for hours (forecast error replaces the horizon error) and a model times larger at every roll; the closing rule at still matters a little, which is why the cyclic end at loses 350 on the toy (the final window must end full).

Step 5 — Fix 2, the terminal value: the sweep

With in the objective (formulation (d)), stationarity gives , so whenever is interior: the price on the last kWh is chosen instead of revealed. The battery keeps each kWh whose best selling price today is below and sells the others, so on the toy only the position of relative to 60 and 80 matters:

At and exactly the battery is indifferent and a solver may return either neighbouring column; the dashboard's “set to the benchmark's ” button adds 0.01 for this reason and can therefore over-store by one step.

  • The right is tomorrow's marginal value of a kWh, the benchmark's : below 60 when tomorrow repeats today, between 60 and 80 when it starts dear. Set from the benchmark, the terminal value reproduces its first day. Would it still be right the day after? Only if recalibrated — is a forecast written as a price, and the calibration is the whole difficulty. In hydro scheduling this price is the water value, computed by a long-horizon model and handed to the short-horizon one.
  • One price is crude when tomorrow's marginal value falls with the amount kept. Against (80, 60, 30, 20) that curve is 80 for the first 10 kWh and 60 beyond, and the benchmark keeps 5–10 kWh; a flat either keeps 5 ( between 60 and 80) or 15 () — it cannot stop at 10. The value curve of section 8 fixes this exactly: on the first 10 kWh and beyond makes the model indifferent between 5 and 10 kWh and sell the rest — the benchmark's own set, because the curve is of the theory above.
  • Against the look-ahead. The terminal value is one LP over hours, no forecast to run, no larger model; the look-ahead is times the model with a forecast to maintain. When the after- value is stable — a repeating daily pattern, a reservoir — wins on cost; when tomorrow can flip from cheap-first to dear-first, only the look-ahead sees it coming.

What to take from the experiment

  • Every closing rule is a guess of tomorrow's marginal-value curve : zero (free end), a quantity (minimum level, cyclic), a flat price (terminal value), the forecast's own curve (look-ahead). The benchmark shows which guess was right, and its is the number every rule is trying to hit.
  • Regret measures the cost of the wrong guess and is never negative; says in which direction it was wrong; against says by how much the rule mispriced the last kWh — with the caveat that at a kink the benchmark price is an interval.
  • On the toy the stakes are 100–750 DKK on a 750-DKK day. On the 24-hour class day starting half full, the cyclic rule costs 80 DKK of regret when tomorrow repeats today (benchmark 5 725 over two days, ending day 1 empty; preset C2d) and 292 DKK when tomorrow has a dear early night; the free end costs 775 on that second tomorrow, and only or reproduce its benchmark (5 940; preset C2e). The size of the mistake scales with the spread between the last hours of today and the first hours of tomorrow, and with the energy the battery can carry across .
  • Look ahead at least one cycle of the battery; calibrate from a longer model and recalibrate it when the pattern changes; use a hard end level only when feasibility after is non-negotiable.

10A family of intertemporal constraints

The battery is one member of a family: constraints that couple the decisions of different periods, so that the problem cannot be solved hour by hour. For each, the question of this lecture is the same — what does the coupling constraint's multiplier mean, and does the coupling keep the problem a linear program, so that the multiplier reading survives?

Storage dynamics and the end of the horizon · LP

, with bounds on and a condition on . The multiplier is the value of a kWh in the battery; it is a step function pinned at the full and empty hours, and its last value is the price the end condition puts on the future. This lecture.

Ramping limits · LP

for a generator. Linear, so the economic dispatch stays an LP. The multiplier of a binding ramp is the value of one more MW/h of ramping capability, and it links the prices of neighbouring hours: a unit that must start climbing in hour to serve hour makes hour dearer than its own merit order would say. Scarcity in one hour propagates to its neighbours.

Daily energy requirement · LP

(a flexible demand, an electric vehicle that must be charged by morning) or (a hydro reservoir with a daily water budget). One constraint for the whole day, so one multiplier: a constant value of energy across the hours, the battery's without the bounds that make it step. The unit runs in the cheapest (or dearest) hours until the requirement is met, and the multiplier is the price of the last hour it uses.

Unit-commitment logic · MILP

On/off status , minimum up and down times (once started, a unit stays on for hours: for ), start-up costs with , and . The binaries make the feasible set non-convex: no KKT conditions, no strong duality, and the market price is no longer a multiplier of the problem solved — it has to be recovered from a linear relaxation or from the LP with the commitment fixed, with side payments for the difference.

The first three couplings are linear: strong duality holds, every constraint has a price and everything in sections 5–8 applies to them with the same steps — write the Lagrangian, read the stationarity condition of the coupled variable, find where the bounds bind. The fourth needs integer variables, and with them the clean link between the optimum and its prices is lost; that is the subject of the unit-commitment lectures. The end-of-horizon question, however, returns there unchanged: a unit that is on at carries a minimum up time into the next day, and a model that does not price it will start units it should not.

11Takeaways

  1. Same duality as week 4, one new coupling. The dynamics constraint links the hours, and its multiplier is the value of a kWh in the battery — a price the optimisation reveals, as the economic dispatch reveals . It is not an input.
  2. is a step function. Constant while the state of charge is interior, it steps up by where the battery is full and down by where it is empty. The battery charges when , discharges when , and is idle in the band between — a band that losses open and that closes to a single line without them. Read as a dispatch of the stored kWh: the marginal hour is the marginal generator of the economic dispatch, and a full or empty hour is a congested line between two hours.
  3. The multipliers of the bounds are sizing signals. is the value of one more kWh of capacity per day and of one more kW; both are slopes of the profit, valid until the next kink. The best duration follows the length of the price events.
  4. Every end-of-horizon condition is a price on the last kWh. Zero with a free end, revealed from today's prices with a minimum or cyclic level, chosen with a terminal value, from a forecast with a rolling horizon. Judge them against the two-day benchmark by regret, terminal state of charge and implicit price (section 9) — and look ahead at least one full cycle of the battery.
  5. Storage, ramping and energy requirements keep the LP; on/off logic does not. As long as the coupling is linear, the whole KKT reading of this lecture carries over; binaries break it, which is where unit commitment starts.
